name: Social media manager
blurb: Plan, post and report on social accounts for local businesses or brands on a monthly fee
title: Social Media Management Business: How to Start and Get Clients
description: How a social media manager earns money, what you need to start a social media management business, who it suits, the risks and how to test it.
h1: How to start a social media management business
answer: A social media manager runs a business's accounts: planning content, creating or editing posts, scheduling, replying to comments and messages, and reporting on results. Most charge a monthly retainer for a set scope, with ads management or content shoots as extras. The catch is that clients often expect sales, not just posts, and they cancel quickly when results are slow or budgets tighten.

sections.h: How a social media manager makes money
body: The usual model is a monthly package defined by platforms, posts per week and response times, sometimes with a setup fee. Paid-ads management, photo or video shoots and one-off strategy sessions are billed separately.

What eats the margin: unlimited revisions, client approvals that take days, scheduling and design tool subscriptions, and the hidden hours of replying to comments and messages. Clearly priced packages protect your time.

ul: A phone that takes good photos and video, a laptop, and design and scheduling tools (many have free tiers).
Working knowledge of the platforms your clients use, including their ad tools and analytics.
Writing and basic editing skills, plus a sense of what fits each brand.
A contract covering deliverables, approval process, who owns the accounts and content, response hours and notice period.
Knowledge of advertising disclosure rules where you work; in the US, the Federal Trade Commission expects paid or gifted endorsements to be clearly disclosed.
Self-employment registration and tax records as your country requires.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Creative people who also like planning and data
Anyone who wants to post only when inspired
Good communicators who can manage client expectations
People who take negative feedback personally
Someone who knows local businesses or one industry
Those unwilling to check messages outside a 9-to-5

ul: Client churn: monthly retainers end easily. Report on results the client cares about (enquiries, bookings, sales), not just likes.
Algorithm and platform changes can cut reach without warning, and clients may blame you.
Account access: never let a business depend on your personal login. Use the platforms' business managers so the client owns the account.
Scope creep: "just one more post" or weekend replies add up. Price extras in writing.
Low-price competition and AI-generated posts make generic content cheap; your value is strategy, consistency and community work.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Run one account seriously for a month, your own or a friend's business, and record the before and after.
Audit the social accounts of ten local businesses and note the ones that clearly need help.
Offer three of them a short free audit with concrete suggestions.
Offer a one-month trial package at a fixed price to anyone interested.
Time the work for that month; if the price would not cover your hours, rethink the package.
Choose one or two platforms and one type of client to focus on.
Create two or three priced packages and a contract template.
Build a short case study from your trial account.
Set up a content calendar and an approval routine before the first post.
Send each client a short monthly report tied to their business goals.
Ask happy clients for referrals and a testimonial.

faq.q: Do I need a degree to be a social media manager?
faq.a: Not to freelance. Clients judge you on results and examples. Courses can help with skills, but a real account you have grown is the strongest proof.

faq.q: How many clients can one social media manager handle?
faq.a: It depends entirely on the scope of each package. Track your hours per client for a couple of months before taking on more, so quality and response times do not slip.

faq.q: Should I also run paid ads for clients?
faq.a: Ads management can be valuable, but it carries responsibility for client money. Learn it on small budgets first and agree in writing who approves spending.
